cards.a: It divides a network into multiple subnets where every subnet uses the same subnet mask/prefix length; this makes subnetting simple and predictable but can waste IP addresses when different subnets have different host requirements.

cards.q: How does FLSM divide 10.1.0.0/16 into /24 subnets?
cards.a: Borrowed bits = 24 − 16 = 8; number of subnets = 2^8 = 256; addresses per subnet = 2^(32−24) = 256; usable hosts per subnet = 256 − 2 = 254; the subnets run 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.255.0/24, all equal-sized.

cards.q: What is the FLSM subnetting formula?
cards.a: Number of subnets = 2^(n − p), total addresses per subnet = 2^(32 − n), traditional usable hosts per subnet = 2^(32 − n) − 2, where p is the original prefix and n is the new subnet prefix length.

cards.q: Work out the FLSM division of 10.10.0.0/16 into /20 subnets.
cards.a: Borrowed bits = 20 − 16 = 4; number of subnets = 2^4 = 16; addresses per subnet = 2^(32−20) = 4096; usable hosts per subnet = 4096 − 2 = 4094.

cards.q: Give the FLSM table for dividing a /24 into /25 through /30.
cards.a: /24 = 1 subnet with 254 hosts; /25 = 2 subnets with 126; /26 = 4 with 62; /27 = 8 with 30; /28 = 16 with 14; /29 = 32 with 6; /30 = 64 subnets with 2 usable hosts each; each additional borrowed bit doubles the subnets and approximately halves addresses per subnet.

cards.q: How many /27 subnets come from a /24 and what is the boundary pattern?
cards.a: Borrowed bits 27 − 24 = 3, so 2^3 = 8 subnets, each with 32 addresses and 30 usable hosts: 192.168.10.0/27, .32/27, .64/27, .96/27, .128/27, .160/27, .192/27, and .224/27; for example .0/27 has usable .1–.30 and broadcast .31.

cards.q: Why does FLSM waste addresses when needs differ?
cards.a: All subnets must use the same mask; if departments need 6, 20, and 100 hosts and a /25 is selected, every department gets 126 usable addresses. VLSM solves this with a /29, /27, and /25 respectively.

FLSM uses the same mask on every subnet with equal sizes, simpler calculation, lower address efficiency when requirements differ, best for uniform requirements, main idea uniformity; VLSM allows different masks per subnet with variable sizes, more planning, higher efficiency, best for different host requirements, main idea efficiency.

cards.q: If every subnet uses /26 but one subnet needs only 2 hosts, is that FLSM or VLSM?
cards.a: FLSM, because every subnet uses the same prefix length; VLSM would assign smaller prefixes such as /30 to small subnets within the same address space.
No; if every subnet has approximately the same host requirement, FLSM can be perfectly efficient for that design — the waste occurs when subnets require significantly different numbers of hosts.

cards.q: Is there a special Cisco command for FLSM?
cards.a: No; there is no ip address flsm command. FLSM is an addressing/subnetting design method, and the CLI configuration looks the same as VLSM, e.g. multiple VLANs all configured with 255.255.255.192 (/26).

No; FLSM simply means subnets use a uniform prefix length. Using the same mask does not automatically make a routing protocol classful, and FLSM works fine with classless protocols such as OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, and BGP.

cards.q: Is FLSM the same as route summarization?
cards.a: No; FLSM concerns how a network's subnets are divided (all sharing the same prefix length), while route summarization concerns representing multiple routes with one summary route, e.g. four /24s 10.1.0.0/24–10.1.3.0/24 summarized as 10.1.0.0/22.

cards.q: State the FLSM quick review points and one-line memory rule.
cards.a: FLSM = same subnet mask for every subnet; advantage simple and predictable; disadvantage can waste addresses; number of subnets = 2^borrowed bits; addresses per subnet = 2^host bits; usable hosts = 2^host bits − 2; /24 → /27 = 8 subnets of 30 hosts; no special CLI; one-line rule: Fixed-Length = Fixed/equal subnet size = same mask everywhere.

cards.q: What is the FLSM vs VLSM decision mental model?
cards.a: Ask: is the same mask used everywhere? If yes, it is FLSM, favoring simplicity and uniformity; if no, it is VLSM, favoring flexibility and address efficiency.
